intro: Welcome to C1! You already know the third conditional: If I had known, I would have come. Today you'll meet its formal twin, Had I known, and other ways to turn a sentence around for emphasis: Never have I seen…, Not only does she…, Rarely do we… You'll also learn when this sounds powerful (a speech, a formal email) and when it just sounds strange (a WhatsApp to a friend).
teachingNotes: Recap in one line, don't re-teach: from b2-third-conditional the learner knows if + had + third form, would have + third form (that lesson said Had I known comes later: this is that lesson), from b1-second-conditional If I were…, and question word order (auxiliary before subject: Have you seen…? Does she speak…?). New: inversion = the auxiliary (have/has/had, do/does/did, am/is/are/was/were, will, can, should…) moves in front of the subject, as in a question, but the sentence is a STATEMENT (full stop, falling intonation). Explain it in Indonesian as 'kata kerja bantu pindah ke depan subjek'. Indonesian trap: Indonesian can also put belum pernah / jarang / tidak hanya first, but the rest stays the same (Belum pernah saya melihat…), so learners write *Never I have seen such a mess / *Rarely we meet, or simply avoid inversion and forget the auxiliary.

Negative inversion (objective use-negative-inversion): Never have I…, Rarely / Seldom do we…, Not only does she… but she also…, Hardly / Scarcely had I… when…, No sooner had I… than…, Under no circumstances should…, Only after / Only when + time… did…, Little did I know (that)… When there's no auxiliary, add do / does / did and use the base verb: Rarely do we meet (not *Rarely we meet / *Rarely meet we), Not only does she speak (not *Not only she speaks / *does she speaks). With be as the main verb there's nothing to add: Rarely is the office this quiet. Partner words don't mix: hardly… when, no sooner… than. With Only after / Only when + a clause, the inversion goes in the MAIN (second) part: Only when I got home did I notice… (not *Only when did I get home / *Only when I got home I noticed). No inversion when the word isn't first (I have never seen…, We only realised later), when it belongs to the subject (Only Budi knew, Hardly anyone came), or when the phrase isn't negative in meaning (Not long ago, I moved to Bandung = recently; In no time, the room was full = very quickly).

Inverted conditionals (objective use-inverted-conditionals): only had, should and were do this. Had + subject + third form = If … had … (Had I known, I would have come; also in mixed conditionals). Should + subject + base verb = If … (should) … for a possible future, polite and formal, very common in business emails and notices: Should you have any questions, please contact us (= Apabila ada pertanyaan…); the result is usually an imperative or will. Were + subject + to + verb (Were I to accept the offer, I would have to move) and Were + subject + noun / adjective (Were I the minister, …) = If … were; Were it not for + noun = If it weren't for (now / in general), Had it not been for + noun = If it hadn't been for (past). Common errors: *If had I known (no if with inversion); *Hadn't I known (negative: not goes after the subject and isn't contracted: Had I not known, Should you not wish, Were it not for); *Was I to… (were for every person); other verbs can't move (*Knew I the answer, *Did I know the answer, I would…).

Register (objective choose-when-to-invert): inversion is never required; the normal word order is always correct. It adds emphasis, drama or formality: speeches, formal letters and emails, reports, news, presentations, storytelling for effect (Little did I know…). In WhatsApp, small talk, chatting with friends or family it sounds dramatic, stiff or like a joke (Never have I tasted such good coffee!), and Should you need… to a friend sounds like a bank. Be honest about the grey areas: Not only… but also… is common in presentations; Had I known also appears in careful speech; Little did I know is fine when telling a story. Only test clear cases: a speech, a formal email or a sign vs a WhatsApp to a friend or chatting with the ojek driver.

Limits: don't teach inversion after place expressions (Here comes the bus, On the table lay a letter), so / such inversion (So tired was I that…), Not until… did… (accept it if the learner uses it correctly: same pattern as Only after), or as / than inversion. No cleft sentences (It was Budi who…), no subjunctive (I suggest that he be…): those are other C1 lessons. The game name 'Never have I ever' is a fixed playful phrase. C1 contexts: speeches at universities and ministries, press conferences, formal emails to partners, reports, NGOs, startups, Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya, Yogyakarta, rupiah.

keyPoints.title: Negative inversion: a negative word first, then auxiliary + subject
keyPoints.explanation: When a negative or limiting word opens the sentence (never, rarely, seldom, not only, hardly, no sooner, under no circumstances, only after / only when, little), the auxiliary moves in front of the subject, like in a question, but it's a statement: Never have I seen such a mess. If there's no auxiliary, add do / does / did and use the base verb: Rarely do we meet, Not only does she speak French, but she also speaks Spanish. Partner words: Hardly had I… when…, No sooner had I… than… With Only after / Only when, invert the second part: Only when I got home did I notice it. Indonesian keeps 'saya melihat' after belum pernah, so the typical mistake is *Never I have seen.

examples.en: Never have I worked with such a talented team.
examples.id: Belum pernah saya bekerja dengan tim seberbakat ini.

examples.en: Not only does Sari speak Mandarin, but she also writes it.
examples.id: Sari tidak hanya bisa berbicara bahasa Mandarin, tetapi juga menulisnya.

examples.en: No sooner had the train left than it started to rain.
examples.id: Begitu keretanya berangkat, langsung turun hujan.

id.title: Inversi negatif: kata negatif di depan, lalu kata kerja bantu + subjek
id.explanation: Kalau kalimat dibuka dengan kata negatif atau pembatas (never, rarely, seldom, not only, hardly, no sooner, under no circumstances, only after / only when, little), kata kerja bantu pindah ke depan subjek, seperti di pertanyaan, tapi kalimatnya tetap pernyataan: Never have I seen such a mess. Kalau tidak ada kata kerja bantu, tambahkan do / does / did dan pakai kata kerja bentuk dasar: Rarely do we meet, Not only does she speak French, but she also speaks Spanish. Pasangan kata: Hardly had I… when…, No sooner had I… than… Dengan Only after / Only when, yang dibalik adalah bagian kedua: Only when I got home did I notice it. Bahasa Indonesia tetap memakai 'saya melihat' setelah belum pernah, jadi kesalahan khasnya *Never I have seen.

keyPoints.title: Inverted conditionals: Had I known, Should you need, Were it not for
keyPoints.explanation: In formal English you can drop if and start with had, should or were. Had I known = If I had known (an imagined past). Should you need help = If you need help (a possible future, polite: common in business emails). Were I to accept = If I were to accept; Were it not for your help = If it weren't for your help (imagined). Never use if as well (*If had I known). Negative: not goes after the subject and isn't shortened: Had I not known (not *Hadn't I known). Were is used for every person: Were she to leave (not *Was she to leave).

examples.en: Had I known about the strike, I would have worked from home.
examples.id: Seandainya waktu itu saya tahu soal mogok kerjanya, saya pasti bekerja dari rumah.

examples.en: Should you need any help, please contact our office in Surabaya.
examples.id: Apabila Anda memerlukan bantuan, silakan hubungi kantor kami di Surabaya.

examples.en: Were it not for the volunteers, the festival would be impossible.
examples.id: Kalau bukan karena para relawan, festival ini tidak mungkin terlaksana.

id.title: Conditional dengan inversi: Had I known, Should you need, Were it not for
id.explanation: Dalam bahasa Inggris formal, kamu bisa membuang if dan memulai dengan had, should atau were. Had I known = If I had known (masa lalu khayalan). Should you need help = If you need help (kemungkinan di masa depan, sopan: sering di email bisnis). Were I to accept = If I were to accept; Were it not for your help = If it weren't for your help (khayalan). Jangan pernah tambahkan if lagi (*If had I known). Negatif: not diletakkan setelah subjek dan tidak disingkat: Had I not known (bukan *Hadn't I known). Were dipakai untuk semua orang: Were she to leave (bukan *Was she to leave).

keyPoints.title: When to invert: speeches and formal writing, not WhatsApp
keyPoints.explanation: Inversion is never required: the normal word order is always correct. Inversion adds emphasis, drama or formality, so it suits speeches, formal letters and emails, reports, news and telling a story for effect (Little did I know…). In a quick WhatsApp, chatting with friends or ordering food it sounds dramatic, stiff or like a joke: write I've never been so tired!, not Never have I been so tired! Should you need anything… fits a company email; to a friend, just write If you need anything, tell me.

examples.en: Never before has our city hosted so many international guests.
examples.id: Belum pernah kota kita menerima tamu internasional sebanyak ini. (pidato wali kota)

examples.en: Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us.
examples.id: Apabila ada pertanyaan, jangan ragu menghubungi kami. (email resmi)

examples.en: If you need the charger, just tell me!
examples.id: Kalau butuh charger, bilang aja! (WhatsApp ke teman: tanpa inversi)

id.title: Kapan memakai inversi: pidato dan tulisan formal, bukan WhatsApp
id.explanation: Inversi tidak pernah wajib: susunan kata biasa selalu benar. Inversi menambah penekanan, kesan dramatis, atau formal, jadi cocok untuk pidato, surat dan email resmi, laporan, berita, dan bercerita supaya berkesan (Little did I know…). Di WhatsApp singkat, ngobrol dengan teman, atau pesan makanan, inversi terdengar dramatis, kaku, atau seperti bercanda: tulis I've never been so tired!, bukan Never have I been so tired! Should you need anything… cocok untuk email perusahaan; ke teman, cukup tulis If you need anything, tell me.

i rarely have breakfast before work

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan has worked at the immigration office in Soekarno-Hatta airport for 25 years. Today he says: 'Never ___ I seen such a long queue!' Write the missing auxiliary.
acceptableAnswers: have
assessment.rubric: Correct: have (Never + present perfect, inverted: have + I + seen; it's about his whole working life up to today). 'had' = 40 (past perfect needs a past reference point; this is today). 'did' = 20 (did + seen is wrong: seen needs have). 'has' = 30 (I takes have). Rewriting it as 'I have never seen' = 30 (correct normal order, but the task is the gap).

assessment.prompt: Rewrite the sentence, starting with Rarely: Our team rarely makes mistakes like this.
acceptableAnswers: rarely does our team make mistakes like this
rarely does our team make a mistake like this
rarely does our team make such mistakes
rarely does our team make mistakes such as this
assessment.rubric: Correct: Rarely does our team make mistakes like this (no auxiliary in the normal sentence, so add does; after does the verb is the base form: make). 'Rarely does our team makes…' = 60 (does + base verb). 'Rarely do our team make…' = 70 (team as a group is possible in British English, but does matches the singular team). 'Rarely our team makes…' = 10 (no inversion: Indonesian order). 'Rarely makes our team…' = 10 (the main verb doesn't move; add does).

assessment.prompt: Complete with one word: No sooner had Bu Ani finished her presentation ___ the questions started.
acceptableAnswers: than
assessment.rubric: Correct: than (No sooner… than… is a fixed pair: begitu…, langsung…). 'when' = 30 (when goes with hardly / scarcely, not with no sooner). 'then' = 40 (a spelling mix-up with than; say so). Any other word = 0.

assessment.prompt: Rewrite the beginning without if: If we had known about the road closure, we would have taken the MRT. → ___ about the road closure, we would have taken the MRT. Write only the missing words.
acceptableAnswers: had we known
had we known about the road closure we would have taken the mrt
had we known about the road closure we'd have taken the mrt
assessment.rubric: Correct: Had we known (if disappears and had moves in front of we; known stays). 'If had we known' = 20 (no if with inversion). 'Did we know' / 'Knew we' = 0 (only had, should and were move). 'Had we know' = 60 (the third form is known). 'We had known' = 10 (that's a fact, not a condition).

assessment.prompt: Make this line from a formal email to a partner in Singapore more formal. Start with Should: If you require any further information about the contract, please contact Bu Ani. → ___ any further information about the contract, please contact Bu Ani. Write only the missing words.
acceptableAnswers: should you require
should you require any further information about the contract please contact bu ani
assessment.rubric: Correct: Should you require (should + subject + base verb = if you require, polite and formal). 'Should you requires' / 'Should you required' = 50 (after should, the base verb). 'If should you require' = 20 (no if). 'Should you need' = 70 (natural and correct, but the sentence uses require). 'You should require' = 0 (that means 'kamu seharusnya memerlukan', not a condition).

assessment.prompt: Rewrite the beginning without if, keeping the negative: If we had not received the grant, the project would have stopped. → ___ the grant, the project would have stopped. Write only the missing words.
acceptableAnswers: had we not received
had we not received the grant the project would have stopped
assessment.rubric: Correct: Had we not received (in an inverted conditional, not goes after the subject and isn't shortened). 'Hadn't we received' = 30 (sounds like a negative question, not a condition). 'If had we not received' = 20 (no if). 'Had not we received' = 40 (not goes after the subject; 'Had not' + subject is old-fashioned and very unusual with a pronoun). 'Had we not receive' = 60 (third form: received).

assessment.prompt: After lunch, Dimas sent this WhatsApp to his best friend: 'Never have I eaten such good bakso!' It sounds like a speech. Rewrite it in the normal word order a friend would use.
acceptableAnswers: i have never eaten such good bakso
i've never eaten such good bakso
i have never had such good bakso
i've never had such good bakso
i have never eaten such good bakso before
i've never eaten such good bakso before
i have never eaten bakso this good
i've never eaten bakso this good
i've never had bakso this good
assessment.rubric: Correct: I have / I've never eaten such good bakso (subject first, have after it, never before the main verb; the meaning stays the same). Minor changes (had instead of eaten, adding before, bakso this good) are fine. 'I never have eaten…' = 60 (never goes after have). 'Never I have eaten…' = 10 (the Indonesian-order mistake). Keeping the inversion = 0 (the task is to make it sound like a friend).

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** in the third conditional you learnt *If I had known, I would have come.* That lesson said the shorter *Had I known…* would come later. Here it is, with its whole family.

**Inversion** means changing the usual order of the **subject** (who does it: *I, we, the ministry*) and the **auxiliary** (the helping verb: *have, has, had, do, does, did, am, is, are, was, were, will, can, should*). The auxiliary jumps **in front of** the subject, just like in a question:
- Question: *Have you seen it?*
- Normal statement: *I have **never** seen such a mess.*
- Inversion: ***Never have I** seen such a mess.*

But inversion is **not a question**. It ends with a full stop (or an exclamation mark), and your voice goes **down** at the end. It's a way to **emphasise** something (memberi penekanan) and to sound formal or dramatic.

It happens in two places: after a **negative or limiting word at the start** (*never, rarely, not only…*) and in **conditionals without if** (*Had I known…*).

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat:** di third conditional kamu belajar *If I had known, I would have come.* Pelajaran itu bilang bentuk yang lebih pendek, *Had I known…*, akan dipelajari nanti. Inilah dia, bersama seluruh 'keluarganya'.

**Inversi** artinya mengubah urutan biasa antara **subjek** (siapa yang melakukan: *I, we, the ministry*) dan **kata kerja bantu** (auxiliary: *have, has, had, do, does, did, am, is, are, was, were, will, can, should*). Kata kerja bantu pindah **ke depan** subjek, persis seperti di kalimat tanya:
- Pertanyaan: *Have you seen it?*
- Pernyataan biasa: *I have **never** seen such a mess.*
- Inversi: ***Never have I** seen such a mess.*

Tapi inversi **bukan pertanyaan**. Kalimatnya diakhiri titik (atau tanda seru), dan suaramu **turun** di akhir. Ini cara untuk **memberi penekanan** dan terdengar formal atau dramatis.

Inversi muncul di dua tempat: setelah **kata negatif atau pembatas di awal kalimat** (*never, rarely, not only…*) dan di **conditional tanpa if** (*Had I known…*).

blocks.text:
**The Indonesian trap.** Indonesian can also put the negative word first: *Belum pernah **saya melihat** kekacauan seperti ini.* But after *belum pernah* the order stays the same: *saya melihat*. So learners translate word by word and write *Never I have seen such a mess* ✗. In English, the auxiliary must jump: ***Never have I** seen such a mess* ✓.
Only the **auxiliary** moves. The main verb stays after the subject: *Never have I **seen*** (not *Never have seen I*).

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia.** Bahasa Indonesia juga bisa menaruh kata negatif di depan: *Belum pernah **saya melihat** kekacauan seperti ini.* Tapi setelah *belum pernah*, urutannya tetap sama: *saya melihat*. Jadi pelajar menerjemahkan kata per kata dan menulis *Never I have seen such a mess* ✗. Dalam bahasa Inggris, kata kerja bantunya harus pindah: ***Never have I** seen such a mess* ✓.
Hanya **kata kerja bantu** yang pindah. Kata kerja utamanya tetap setelah subjek: *Never have I **seen*** (bukan *Never have seen I*).

options: Never I have been so nervous before a presentation.
Never have I been so nervous before a presentation.
Never have been I so nervous before a presentation.
blocks.explain: After never at the start, the auxiliary have goes in front of the subject I, and the main verb been stays after it. The first sentence keeps the Indonesian order; the third moves the main verb too.

id.explain: Setelah never di awal kalimat, kata kerja bantu have pindah ke depan subjek I, dan kata kerja utama been tetap di belakangnya. Kalimat pertama memakai urutan bahasa Indonesia; kalimat ketiga ikut memindahkan kata kerja utama.

material.title: Negative openers: do, does, did and partner words

blocks.text:
**No auxiliary? Borrow do / does / did.** In the present simple and past simple there's no helping verb (*We rarely meet. She speaks French. I knew nothing.*). So you add one, exactly as in a question, and the main verb goes back to its **base form** (bentuk dasar):
- *We rarely meet.* → ***Rarely do we meet.*** (not *Rarely we meet* or *Rarely meet we*)
- *She speaks French and Spanish.* → ***Not only does she speak** French, but she also speaks Spanish.* (not *Not only she speaks…*, not *does she speaks*)
- *I had no idea.* → ***Little did I know** that he was the new director.*

With **be** as the main verb, there's nothing to add: be moves by itself: ***Rarely is** the office this quiet.*

**Openers with a partner word** (for one thing happening right after another):
- ***Hardly** had I sat down **when** the phone rang.* (*Scarcely… when* is the same)
- ***No sooner** had I sat down **than** the phone rang.*
Don't mix the partners: *hardly… when*, *no sooner… than*.

**Only after / Only when + time:** the inversion goes in the **second** part: *Only when I got home **did I notice** the missing file.* (not *Only when did I get home…*, not *Only when I got home I noticed…*)

id.text:
**Tidak ada kata kerja bantu? Pinjam do / does / did.** Di present simple dan past simple tidak ada kata kerja bantu (*We rarely meet. She speaks French. I knew nothing.*). Jadi kamu menambahkannya, persis seperti di kalimat tanya, dan kata kerja utamanya kembali ke **bentuk dasar**:
- *We rarely meet.* → ***Rarely do we meet.*** (bukan *Rarely we meet* atau *Rarely meet we*)
- *She speaks French and Spanish.* → ***Not only does she speak** French, but she also speaks Spanish.* (bukan *Not only she speaks…*, bukan *does she speaks*)
- *I had no idea.* → ***Little did I know** that he was the new director.*

Kalau kata kerja utamanya **be**, tidak perlu menambah apa-apa: be pindah sendiri: ***Rarely is** the office this quiet.*

**Pembuka dengan pasangan kata** (untuk satu hal yang terjadi tepat setelah hal lain):
- ***Hardly** had I sat down **when** the phone rang.* (*Scarcely… when* sama saja)
- ***No sooner** had I sat down **than** the phone rang.*
Jangan tertukar pasangannya: *hardly… when*, *no sooner… than*.

**Only after / Only when + waktu:** inversinya ada di bagian **kedua**: *Only when I got home **did I notice** the missing file.* (bukan *Only when did I get home…*, bukan *Only when I got home I noticed…*)

rows.en: Rarely do we get feedback this detailed.
rows.id: Jarang sekali kami mendapat masukan sedetail ini.

rows.id: Rina sama sekali tidak tahu bahwa atasannya sedang mendengarkan.

blocks.text:
**When a negative word does NOT cause inversion** (so these don't break the rule):
- The word isn't first: *I have never seen…*, *We only realised it later.* (normal order)
- The word belongs to the **subject**: *Only Budi knew the password.* *Hardly anyone came.* (here *only Budi* and *hardly anyone* ARE the subject, so there's nothing to swap)
- The phrase isn't really negative: *Not long ago, I moved to Bandung* (= recently). *In no time, the room was full* (= very quickly).
**Little** at the start means *sama sekali tidak*, not *sedikit*: *Little did I know* = I had no idea.

id.text:
**Kapan kata negatif TIDAK menyebabkan inversi** (jadi contoh ini tidak melanggar aturan):
- Katanya tidak di awal: *I have never seen…*, *We only realised it later.* (urutan biasa)
- Katanya bagian dari **subjek**: *Only Budi knew the password.* *Hardly anyone came.* (di sini *only Budi* dan *hardly anyone* ADALAH subjeknya, jadi tidak ada yang ditukar)
- Ungkapannya sebenarnya tidak negatif: *Not long ago, I moved to Bandung* (= baru-baru ini). *In no time, the room was full* (= cepat sekali).
**Little** di awal kalimat artinya *sama sekali tidak*, bukan *sedikit*: *Little did I know* = saya sama sekali tidak tahu.

options: Not only she manages the team, but she also writes the code.
Not only does she manages the team, but she also writes the code.
Not only does she manage the team, but she also writes the code.
blocks.explain: She manages has no auxiliary, so add does before she, and after does the verb goes back to the base form: manage. The first sentence has no inversion (Indonesian order); the second keeps the -s after does.

id.explain: She manages tidak punya kata kerja bantu, jadi tambahkan does sebelum she, dan setelah does kata kerjanya kembali ke bentuk dasar: manage. Kalimat pertama tidak memakai inversi (urutan bahasa Indonesia); kalimat kedua masih memakai -s setelah does.

material.title: Conditionals without if: had, should, were

blocks.text:
In formal English you can **drop if** and start with the auxiliary. Only **three** words do this:
- **Had** + subject + third form = *If … had …* (an imagined past): ***Had I known** about the strike, I would have worked from home.* = If I had known…
- **Should** + subject + base verb = *If …* (something that may happen; polite and formal, very common in business emails and notices): ***Should you need** any help, please contact our office.* = If you need any help…
- **Were** + subject + *to* + verb, or + a noun / adjective = *If … were* (imagined): ***Were I to accept** the offer, I would have to move to Surabaya.* ***Were I** the director, I would change this rule.*

Two fixed phrases: ***Were it not for** + noun* = *If it weren't for* (kalau bukan karena, now or in general), and ***Had it not been for** + noun* = *If it hadn't been for* (the past).

The second part of the sentence doesn't change: it's the same *would / would have / please / will* as with *if*.

id.text:
Dalam bahasa Inggris formal kamu bisa **membuang if** dan memulai dengan kata kerja bantu. Hanya **tiga** kata yang bisa:
- **Had** + subjek + bentuk ketiga = *If … had …* (masa lalu khayalan): ***Had I known** about the strike, I would have worked from home.* = If I had known…
- **Should** + subjek + bentuk dasar = *If …* (sesuatu yang mungkin terjadi; sopan dan formal, sangat sering di email bisnis dan pengumuman): ***Should you need** any help, please contact our office.* = If you need any help…
- **Were** + subjek + *to* + kata kerja, atau + kata benda / kata sifat = *If … were* (khayalan): ***Were I to accept** the offer, I would have to move to Surabaya.* ***Were I** the director, I would change this rule.*

Dua ungkapan tetap: ***Were it not for** + kata benda* = *If it weren't for* (kalau bukan karena, sekarang atau secara umum), dan ***Had it not been for** + kata benda* = *If it hadn't been for* (masa lalu).

Bagian kedua kalimatnya tidak berubah: tetap *would / would have / please / will* seperti dengan *if*.

blocks.text:
**Three traps:**
1. **No if.** The auxiliary at the front already means *if*: *If had I known* ✗ → ***Had I known*** ✓.
2. **Negative: not after the subject, never shortened.** ***Had I not known*** ✓, ***Should you not wish** to attend* ✓. *Hadn't I known* ✗ sounds like a negative question (*Bukankah saya sudah tahu?*).
3. **Only had, should, were.** Other verbs can't do this: *Knew I the answer* ✗, *Did I know the answer, I would…* ✗ → *If I knew the answer…* (only *had*, *should* and *were* can move)
Indonesian formal letters have a perfect match for *should*: ***Apabila** Bapak/Ibu memerlukan informasi lebih lanjut…* = ***Should** you need further information…*

id.text:
**Tiga jebakan:**
1. **Tanpa if.** Kata kerja bantu di depan sudah berarti *if*: *If had I known* ✗ → ***Had I known*** ✓.
2. **Negatif: not setelah subjek, tidak pernah disingkat.** ***Had I not known*** ✓, ***Should you not wish** to attend* ✓. *Hadn't I known* ✗ terdengar seperti pertanyaan negatif (*Bukankah saya sudah tahu?*).
3. **Hanya had, should, were.** Kata kerja lain tidak bisa: *Knew I the answer* ✗, *Did I know the answer, I would…* ✗ → *If I knew the answer…* (hanya *had*, *should* dan *were* yang bisa pindah)
Surat resmi bahasa Indonesia punya padanan yang pas untuk *should*: ***Apabila** Bapak/Ibu memerlukan informasi lebih lanjut…* = ***Should** you need further information…*

material.title: Powerful or strange? Choosing when to invert

blocks.text:
**Inversion is never required.** The normal word order is **always correct**: *I have never seen…*, *If you need help…*. Inversion is a choice of **style**: it adds emphasis, drama or formality.

**Where it sounds natural:**
- speeches and presentations (*Never before has our university…*)
- formal letters, emails and notices (*Should you have any questions…*, *Under no circumstances should…*)
- reports, news and academic writing (*Not only did sales rise, but costs also fell.*)
- telling a story for effect, even with friends (*Little did I know that…*)

**Where it sounds strange:** a quick WhatsApp, chatting with friends or family, ordering food, talking to the ojek driver. There it sounds **dramatic**, **stiff** (kaku) or like a **joke**. *Never have I been so hungry!* to your sister sounds like a TV drama.

Some patterns are more everyday than others: *Not only… but also…* is common in presentations, and *Had I known…* appears in careful speech. But *Should you need…* in a chat with a friend sounds like a letter from the bank.

id.text:
**Inversi tidak pernah wajib.** Susunan kata biasa **selalu benar**: *I have never seen…*, *If you need help…*. Inversi adalah pilihan **gaya**: menambah penekanan, kesan dramatis, atau formal.

**Di mana terdengar alami:**
- pidato dan presentasi (*Never before has our university…*)
- surat, email, dan pengumuman resmi (*Should you have any questions…*, *Under no circumstances should…*)
- laporan, berita, dan tulisan akademis (*Not only did sales rise, but costs also fell.*)
- bercerita supaya berkesan, bahkan dengan teman (*Little did I know that…*)

**Di mana terdengar aneh:** WhatsApp singkat, ngobrol dengan teman atau keluarga, pesan makanan, bicara dengan sopir ojek. Di situ inversi terdengar **dramatis**, **kaku**, atau seperti **bercanda**. *Never have I been so hungry!* ke adikmu terdengar seperti sinetron.

Ada pola yang lebih umum dipakai sehari-hari: *Not only… but also…* sering di presentasi, dan *Had I known…* muncul dalam ucapan yang hati-hati. Tapi *Should you need…* saat chat dengan teman terdengar seperti surat dari bank.

blocks.text: **Indonesian has no such word-order change**, so many learners either **avoid inversion completely** (that's fine in conversation, but formal writing loses some power) or **use it everywhere** to sound advanced (then chats sound like speeches). A simple test: would you say it with a microphone, or write it on letterhead (kop surat)? Then inversion can fit. Would you send it with an emoji? Then use the normal order.

id.text: **Bahasa Indonesia tidak punya perubahan susunan kata seperti ini**, jadi banyak pelajar **menghindari inversi sama sekali** (tidak apa-apa dalam percakapan, tapi tulisan formal kehilangan sebagian kekuatannya) atau **memakainya di mana-mana** supaya terdengar mahir (akhirnya chat terdengar seperti pidato). Tes sederhana: apakah kamu akan mengucapkannya di depan mikrofon, atau menulisnya di kertas berkop surat? Kalau ya, inversi bisa cocok. Apakah kamu akan mengirimnya dengan emoji? Kalau ya, pakai urutan biasa.

blocks.prompt: Where does this sentence fit best? Under no circumstances should visitors enter the laboratory without a mask.
options: A sign on the laboratory door
blocks.explain: Under no circumstances should… is a strong, formal warning: perfect for a sign, a notice or a safety briefing. To a housemate you would just say Don't go in without a mask!

id.prompt: Kalimat ini paling cocok di mana? Under no circumstances should visitors enter the laboratory without a mask.
id.explain: Under no circumstances should… adalah larangan yang tegas dan formal: pas untuk papan peringatan, pengumuman, atau pengarahan keselamatan. Ke teman kos, cukup bilang Don't go in without a mask!

id.intro: Selamat datang di C1! Kamu sudah kenal third conditional: If I had known, I would have come. Hari ini kamu bertemu 'kembaran' formalnya, Had I known, dan cara lain membalik susunan kalimat untuk memberi penekanan: Never have I seen…, Not only does she…, Rarely do we… Kamu juga akan belajar kapan inversi terdengar berkesan (pidato, email resmi) dan kapan justru terdengar aneh (WhatsApp ke teman).
suggestedQuestions: Apakah 'Never have I seen' itu pertanyaan? Kenapa bentuknya mirip pertanyaan?
Kenapa kita menambahkan do di 'Rarely do we meet' tapi tidak di 'Never have I seen'?
Apa bedanya 'Hardly had I… when' dan 'No sooner had I… than'?

assessment.inv-1: Pak Hasan sudah 25 tahun bekerja di kantor imigrasi Bandara Soekarno-Hatta. Hari ini dia berkata: 'Never ___ I seen such a long queue!' Tulis kata kerja bantu yang hilang.
assessment.inv-2: Tulis ulang kalimat ini, dimulai dengan Rarely: Our team rarely makes mistakes like this.
assessment.inv-3: Lengkapi dengan satu kata: No sooner had Bu Ani finished her presentation ___ the questions started.
assessment.inv-4: Tulis ulang bagian awalnya tanpa if: If we had known about the road closure, we would have taken the MRT. → ___ about the road closure, we would have taken the MRT. Tulis kata-kata yang hilang saja.
assessment.inv-5: Buat kalimat dari email resmi ke mitra di Singapura ini lebih formal. Mulai dengan Should: If you require any further information about the contract, please contact Bu Ani. → ___ any further information about the contract, please contact Bu Ani. Tulis kata-kata yang hilang saja.
assessment.inv-6: Tulis ulang bagian awalnya tanpa if, tetap dalam bentuk negatif: If we had not received the grant, the project would have stopped. → ___ the grant, the project would have stopped. Tulis kata-kata yang hilang saja.
assessment.inv-7: Setelah makan siang, Dimas mengirim WhatsApp ini ke sahabatnya: 'Never have I eaten such good bakso!' Kedengarannya seperti pidato. Tulis ulang dalam susunan kata biasa yang dipakai antarteman, dalam bahasa Inggris.
